followUpQuestions.prompt: Why is checking whether a user has voted in application code not enough to guarantee one vote per poll?
expectedAnswerPoints: Concurrent requests can both pass an application-level check.
A database unique constraint on (poll_id,user_id) is the final integrity guard.
The API should handle unique-constraint conflicts as duplicate submissions.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why might the vote API acknowledge a vote before the displayed poll totals have changed?
expectedAnswerPoints: The durable vote record is committed synchronously.
Counter aggregation can happen asynchronously through a queue and worker.
This reduces request latency while allowing small, explicit result freshness lag.

followUpQuestions.prompt: A queue delivers the same vote event three times. How do you prevent the option count from increasing three times?
expectedAnswerPoints: Use a stable event ID as an idempotency key.
Deduplication and counter increment must be one atomic operation.
A separate check-then-increment sequence can race or fail between steps.

followUpQuestions.prompt: The counter store is lost but all vote records remain in SQL. How would you restore results?
expectedAnswerPoints: Treat counters as derived state, not the source of truth.
Rebuild counts by aggregating durable vote records or replaying a retained event log.
Track rebuild progress and avoid serving incomplete totals as final.

followUpQuestions.prompt: A single live poll receives 50,000 votes per second. How would you reduce contention on a single option counter?
expectedAnswerPoints: Shard each option counter across multiple keys or partitions.
Increment a shard selected by a stable or randomized strategy.
Merge shard values for result reads, optionally caching the merged result.
Consider the added read complexity and freshness trade-off.

referenceSolutions.name: Durable vote records with asynchronous counter aggregation

flows.name: Accept a vote
steps: Client submits a vote to the API.
API attempts to insert a durable vote record with a unique (poll_id,user_id) constraint.
Only after the database commit succeeds does the API publish a vote event to the queue.
The API acknowledges the accepted vote; a duplicate unique-key conflict is returned as already voted.

flows.name: Aggregate and read results
steps: Worker consumes the vote event from the queue.
Worker atomically deduplicates the event ID and increments the option counter.
Client requests results; API reads the per-option totals from the counter store.

flows.name: Recover counters
steps: If the counter store is lost, rebuild option totals from durable vote records or replay retained events.
Use the same event-id deduplication strategy during replay.
Expose rebuild status and reconcile totals before declaring results fully current.

strengths: Database uniqueness protects the one-vote rule under concurrency.
Queue decouples vote acceptance from aggregation work.
Derived counters make result reads inexpensive.
limitations: The API-to-database and API-to-queue dual write can fail between commit and publish; a transactional outbox is a production-grade improvement.
The simplified model treats deduplication plus increment as one atomic counter-store operation.
tradeoffs: Results are eventually consistent by a bounded queue-processing lag rather than updated synchronously on every vote.
Durable vote rows cost more storage than keeping only counters, but enable audit and rebuild.

referenceSolutions.name: Direct API entry with independently scalable aggregation

flows.name: Vote submission
steps: Client calls the stateless Poll API directly; multiple API instances can sit behind the platform's ingress.
API persists a vote with the unique poll_id,user_id constraint.
After commit, API publishes a vote event for background aggregation.

flows.name: Results and recovery
steps: API reads cached counters for result requests.
Workers consume events and use atomic event deduplication before incrementing counters.
Workers can read durable votes to support reconciliation after counter loss.

strengths: API and worker capacity can be scaled independently.
The design keeps the same durable source of truth and asynchronous result path.
limitations: The diagram omits an explicit load balancer or ingress component, which must be provided by deployment infrastructure.
The outbox gap between database commit and queue publish still needs a transactional outbox or reliable publisher in production.
tradeoffs: A smaller logical diagram keeps the core vote path visible but leaves ingress and operational reliability details implicit.

revisionRecommendations.text: Connect the API to durable SQL storage and configure a unique constraint on poll_id,user_id; application-level checks alone are insufficient.
Publish a vote event only after the vote record commits, then connect the queue to a worker and the worker to the counter store.
Serve poll results from the counter store instead of scanning all individual vote records on every request.
Use stable event IDs and an atomic deduplicate-plus-increment operation; retain durable votes for reconciliation.
Set SQL write capacity, queue ingestion capacity and aggregate worker throughput to at least 5,000 votes/sec.
Set counter-store operations capacity to at least 10,000 operations/sec.
Enable worker idempotency and counter-store event deduplication plus atomic increment.
